Background
The Problem

A Desert Isn't Always Made of Sand

In Nevada, the phrase "healthcare desert" rarely evokes the literal landscape — yet for thousands of residents of Clark County, the two are uncomfortably close. Clark County is famous for Las Vegas, one of the most visited cities on Earth, but its census tracts tell a more complicated story. Beyond the Strip's neon glow, the county stretches south and east into some of the most medically underserved terrain in the American West.

This investigation applies a reproducible spatial pipeline to answer a deceptively simple question: which residents face the double burden of high healthcare vulnerability and poor geographic access to care? Using 2022 American Community Survey data, national facility inventories from HRSA and HIFLD, and real drive-time isochrones, we classify every census tract in Clark County into one of four access categories — from Adequate to Desert.

"The communities most likely to need care are least equipped to reach it — separated not just by income or insurance, but by miles of open highway with nowhere to turn."

535 Total census tracts analysed
1 Confirmed healthcare desert tract
2 At-risk tracts (high vulnerability, marginal access)
2 Underserved tracts (moderate vulnerability, poor access)
Methodology
How We Measured It

Two Axes, One Verdict

A census tract qualifies as a healthcare desert along two independent dimensions. The first is a vulnerability index — a weighted composite of four ACS variables that proxy for healthcare need and capacity to travel for care. The second is drive-time access — whether a tract's population centroid falls within a 30-minute drive of any HRSA-listed health center or HIFLD-catalogued hospital, using OpenRouteService road-network isochrones.

Desert

Q4 vulnerability and outside the 30-min isochrone. Highest-need, most isolated.

At Risk

Q4 vulnerability and inside 30-min but outside the 15-min isochrone.

Underserved

Q3 vulnerability and outside the 30-min isochrone. Moderate need, poor access.

Adequate

All other tracts. Not free from problems — but not classified as a desert.

The vulnerability index weights are: uninsured rate (30%), elderly population 65+ (25%), poverty rate (25%), and households with no vehicle (20%). Each variable is min-max normalised across all county tracts before weighting, then quartile-classified. Tracts in the top quartile (Q4) are considered highly vulnerable.

Facilities
The Supply Side

Healthcare Is Clustered Where People Already Have It

The facility map below plots every HRSA-registered community health center and HIFLD-catalogued hospital in the Clark County study area. The pattern is immediately striking: nearly all facilities are concentrated within the urban core of Las Vegas and Henderson. Outlying communities — from Moapa Valley in the north to the southern reaches near Bullhead City — have almost nothing.

This geographic mismatch between supply and demand is the core of the healthcare desert problem. Facilities are located where land is available, funding follows, and staff want to live — not necessarily where vulnerable populations cluster.

Drive-Time Access
Getting There

The Road Network Tells Its Own Story

Straight-line distance to the nearest facility is a misleading metric in a county shaped by desert topography and sparse roads. This analysis uses drive-time isochrones computed via the OpenRouteService API — polygons representing the actual road-network area reachable within 15, 30, and 60 minutes from each facility.

The isochrone map reveals the ragged, dendritic shape of accessibility in Clark County. Tentacles of coverage follow the highway network, while the vast spaces between roads remain unreachable within 30 minutes. The 30-minute threshold aligns with clinical research on care-seeking delays and mirrors common federal definitions of geographic access.

Results
The Classification

Who Lives in a Healthcare Desert?

When vulnerability and geographic access are combined, Clark County's 535 census tracts resolve into a clear spatial pattern. The vast majority — 530 tracts, containing 2.25 million people — fall into the Adequate category. But the tracts that don't tell an important story about where the system fails.

The single confirmed Desert tract, Census Tract 57.03, has a vulnerability score of 0.357 — placing it in the top quartile — with a poverty rate of 24.7%, an elderly share of 38%, an uninsured rate of 11.9%, and 21.7% of households lacking a vehicle. Its 949 residents are beyond a 30-minute drive from any health center or hospital.

Vulnerability Patterns
Intersecting Burdens

Poverty, Insurance, and Geography Lock Together

The correlation matrix in Figure 5 reveals something that should inform policy: the vulnerability variables do not act independently. Uninsured rate and poverty rate have a strong positive correlation (r = 0.65), and no-vehicle households and poverty are even more tightly coupled (r = 0.69). Desert tracts are not merely poor, or merely car-free, or merely uninsured — they are typically all three at once.

Elderly share tells a different story. It correlates negatively with uninsured rate (r = −0.32), likely reflecting Medicare coverage for most Americans over 65. The index captures elderly vulnerability not through insurance gaps but through mobility constraints and chronic care needs.

Implications
What the Data Means

A Small Number With Large Consequences

One desert tract and five "problem" tracts combined might seem like a reassuring headline for a county of 2.3 million people — 99.1% of tracts classified as Adequate. But that framing misses the point. The 949 people in Census Tract 57.03 do not live in a statistic; they live in a place where a medical emergency requires a drive longer than most Americans spend commuting to work, in a community where over a third of residents are elderly, a quarter live below the poverty line, and a fifth of households have no car.

The "At Risk" and "Underserved" designations — 4 additional tracts, roughly 10,700 people — represent the population one policy decision or clinic closure away from full desert status. They are the early warning system.

"99.1% Adequate sounds like success. For the 949 residents of Tract 57.03, it sounds like someone else's county."

The analysis also surfaces a structural insight: the variables that make communities vulnerable to healthcare deserts are tightly correlated. Interventions targeting only one dimension — adding a clinic, subsidising insurance, or expanding transit — may be insufficient. Communities at greatest risk need simultaneous progress on multiple fronts.

Reproducibility
Run It Yourself

This Analysis Is Fully Reproducible

The pipeline that produced every map and statistic in this piece is open-source and configurable. Changing two lines in config.py — STATE_FIPS and COUNTY_FIPS — reruns the entire analysis for any US county. Free API keys from the Census Bureau and OpenRouteService are all that's required.

Two flags make experimentation fast: --skip-isochrones replaces ORS calls with Euclidean buffers for quick iteration, and --county "*" scales the run to all counties in a state. The pipeline caches raw downloads at every step, so reruns are cheap.

■ Data & Methods

This analysis uses the following data sources and techniques:

  • Population data: U.S. Census Bureau ACS 5-Year Estimates (2022) via the census Python package. Variables: B01001 (age/sex), B27001 (insurance status), B17001 (poverty status), B25044 (vehicle availability).
  • Facilities: HRSA Geospatial Data Warehouse (community health centers) and HIFLD (hospitals).
  • Isochrones: OpenRouteService API at 15, 30, and 60-minute thresholds. Euclidean buffer fallback available.
  • Classification: Vulnerability scored via min-max normalisation and weighted sum; quartile-cut with pd.qcut; access determined by centroid-in-polygon spatial join (GeoPandas).
  • Cartography: Static maps via matplotlib + contextily; interactive maps via Folium.

Known limitations: temporal mismatch between ACS 2022 and facility datasets; centroid-based access assignment ignores tract shape; no pre-filtering of facilities to a study-area bounding box.
